testName: ICT3631 · Jan/Feb 2025 Exam · verified command practice
sourceType: Paraphrased practice based on the indexed Jan/Feb 2025 examination. Command answers are cross-checked against standard Linux/Samba tooling.
sourceLimitations: The indexed copy exposes the practical command topics but some IP addresses are truncated by OCR. The app therefore uses synthetic hostnames/addresses while testing the same commands.

questions.text: Write one SSH command that logs in as user `johdoe` on `server1.example` and executes `hostname` on the remote machine without first opening an interactive shell.
aiRubric: Uses ssh.
Specifies johdoe@server1.example or an equivalent user/host form.
Executes hostname as the remote command.
questions.explanation:
SSH can run a command directly after the remote target. The remote command is executed and its output is returned to the local terminal.

Student note: The pattern is `ssh user@host command`.

questions.text: Explain a safe step-by-step method for configuring a Linux log host with rsyslog and sending logs to it from a client.
questions.correctAnswer: On the server, install/enable rsyslog, configure an input for the chosen protocol (commonly UDP or TCP on 514), restrict permitted senders where possible, allow the required firewall port, choose rules/templates for received logs, validate the configuration and restart/enable rsyslog. On each client, configure a forwarding rule to the log host (`@host:514` for UDP or `@@host:514` for TCP in traditional rsyslog syntax), validate/restart, generate a test message with logger, and confirm it arrives. Production designs should prefer authenticated/encrypted transport where available.
aiRubric: Configures rsyslog receiver/input on the log host.
Uses an appropriate transport/port and firewall rule.
Configures a client forwarding rule.
Restarts/enables or reloads rsyslog after validation.
Tests with logger or another controlled message.
Verifies received logs.
Mentions access restriction or secure transport as a production safeguard.
questions.explanation:
Central logging needs both ends: a server that listens and stores messages, and clients that forward them. Testing matters because a configuration can be syntactically valid but still blocked by a firewall or routing problem.

Student note: Answer in order: server → firewall → client → restart → test → verify.

questions.text: Give a modern Linux command that displays addresses and status for all network interfaces.
aiRubric: Uses `ip addr`, `ip address`, or `ip addr show` to display all interfaces.
questions.explanation:
The `ip` command from iproute2 is the modern tool for viewing and managing network interfaces and addresses.

Student note: `ip addr` is the modern replacement you should know even if older material also teaches `ifconfig`.

questions.text: Give a legacy command that can show information for all network interfaces, including inactive ones.
aiRubric: Uses `ifconfig -a`.
questions.explanation:
`ifconfig -a` displays all interfaces on systems where the legacy net-tools package is available.

Student note: On modern Linux, prefer `ip addr`; know `ifconfig -a` because older course material and systems may still use it.

questions.text: Write a command that tests basic IP reachability to a host named `host1`.
aiRubric: Uses ping with host1 (optionally with a safe count such as `-c 4`).
questions.explanation:
`ping` sends ICMP echo requests and is a basic reachability test. A failed ping does not always prove the host is down because ICMP can be filtered.

Student note: Ping is a first test, not a complete diagnosis.

questions.text: If you know host1's IP address, may you normally use that IP address instead of the hostname with `ping`?
questions.explanation:
`ping` can normally target either a resolvable hostname or an IP address. Using the IP can also help separate a DNS problem from a network reachability problem.

Student note: If IP works but hostname fails, investigate name resolution/DNS.

questions.text: Give a Linux command that shows the network path/hops used to reach `google.com`.
aiRubric: Uses `traceroute google.com` or a clearly equivalent route-tracing command such as `tracepath google.com`.
questions.explanation:
A route-tracing tool sends probes with increasing hop limits so it can reveal routers along the path toward the destination.

Student note: `ping` asks 'can I reach it?'; `traceroute` asks 'which path is being taken?'.

questions.text: In a legacy Red Hat-style interface configuration, explain the purpose of `PEERDNS=no`.
questions.correctAnswer: It tells the network configuration not to let DNS information learned from the peer/DHCP connection automatically replace or update the system resolver configuration for that interface. It is used when DNS settings should be managed manually or by another mechanism.
aiRubric: Explains that peer/DHCP-provided DNS should not automatically update resolver DNS settings.
Mentions manual/controlled DNS configuration.
questions.explanation:
The setting is about DNS configuration, not whether the interface itself can connect to the network.

Student note: PEERDNS controls accepting peer-provided DNS information; it does not disable DNS as a service.

questions.text: For a traditional Samba file server, list the main SMB/NetBIOS ports, state whether each uses TCP or UDP, and identify whether `smbd` or `nmbd` is mainly associated with it.
questions.correctAnswer: The standard set expected in this course context is UDP 137 and UDP 138 for NetBIOS name/datagram functions associated with nmbd, plus TCP 139 and TCP 445 for SMB file/session service associated with smbd. Port 445 is direct SMB without the older NetBIOS session layer.
aiRubric: UDP 137 is included and associated with NetBIOS/nmbd.
UDP 138 is included and associated with NetBIOS/nmbd.
TCP 139 is included and associated with SMB/smbd.
TCP 445 is included and associated with direct SMB/smbd.
questions.explanation:
Samba may use the older NetBIOS-related ports as well as direct SMB on TCP 445. Which ports should be exposed in a real network depends on the design and firewall policy.

Student note: Memorise protocol with port: 137/UDP, 138/UDP, 139/TCP, 445/TCP.

questions.text: Write the iptables command that deletes rule number 5 from the INPUT chain.
aiRubric: Uses iptables with `-D INPUT 5`.
questions.explanation:
`-D` deletes a rule. When a rule number is supplied, iptables removes that numbered rule from the named chain.

Student note: List rules with line numbers before deleting in real administration so you do not remove the wrong rule.

questions.text: Write the iptables command that changes the default policy of the INPUT chain to ACCEPT.
aiRubric: Uses iptables with `-P INPUT ACCEPT`.
questions.explanation:
`-P` sets the built-in chain policy. This affects packets that reach the end of the chain without matching a rule.

Student note: Default policy and an appended rule are different things.

questions.text: Write an iptables command that appends an INPUT rule to drop TCP traffic destined for port 22.
aiRubric: Appends to INPUT with `-A INPUT`.
Matches TCP.
Matches destination port 22.
Uses DROP target.
questions.explanation:
The rule matches incoming TCP packets whose destination port is 22 and sends them to the DROP target.

Student note: Order matters in a firewall ruleset. An earlier ACCEPT rule could match before a later DROP rule.

questions.text: Give a command pattern that grants user `sam` read and write ACL permissions on `report.txt`.
aiRubric: Uses setfacl with modify (`-m`) and a user ACL entry granting sam read/write on report.txt.
questions.explanation:
`setfacl` modifies access control list entries. The `u:sam:rw` entry gives user sam read and write ACL permissions.

Student note: ACLs can grant permissions to a named user without changing the file's owner or group.

questions.text: Give the command used to display the ACL entries for `report.txt`.
aiRubric: Uses getfacl on report.txt.
questions.explanation:
`getfacl` displays the file's access control list, including named user and group entries.

Student note: setfacl changes ACLs; getfacl reads them.
